metadata.title: Are European regions on the right track to achieve the 2030 strategic education and training targets? A comprehensive performance assessment

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study does not use student-level ILSA microdata (e.g., PISA/TIMSS/ICILS) with sampling weights or plausible values. Instead, it constructs a regional benchmarking dataset using Eurostat indicators for 2019 at NUTS-I and country levels, treating each region as a decision-making unit (DMU) in a Benefit-of-the-Doubt (BoD) Data Envelopment Analysis framework. Because the analysis is based on aggregated regional statistics rather than survey microdata, there is no complex survey design to weight and no replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife) to apply. Missingness is handled through a complete-data requirement for the seven variables used in the BoD optimization (five ET2030 indicators plus two contextual variables), with the paper stating that imputation should only be performed if reliable; otherwise units are excluded.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent quantities are not cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA with PVs; the study benchmarks regional performance using Eurostat-derived indicator rates (e.g., early childhood education, early leavers, tertiary attainment, lifelong learning, and digital skills proxies) aggregated at NUTS-I/country levels. The paper also does not report a specific missing-data handling method (e.g., listwise deletion vs. imputation strategy) beyond a general rule that units should have complete data for all seven variables and that imputation should be used only if reliable, which is insufficient for a precise schema mapping.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analysis uses 2019 Eurostat data for five ET2030 indicators (Y1–Y5) plus two contextual variables (Z1 unemployment and Z2 citizenship) at NUTS-I and country levels, treating each geography as a DMU. For the BoD optimization, all DMUs must have complete data for all seven variables; the paper states that imputation should only be performed if reliable, otherwise the evaluated unit should be excluded. The final analysis includes 32 countries and 101 NUTS-I regions, with additional sub-categorization of regions into capital and island regions to support within-country disparity analysis. Indicators Y2 (early leavers) and Y5 (low-achieving families in digital skills) are transformed by taking complements (100% minus the original values) so that higher values correspond to better performance across all indicators before entering the optimization model.

Using Eurostat indicators for 2019, it constructs five performance indicators (Y1 early childhood education, Y2 early leavers, Y3 tertiary attainment, Y4 adult lifelong learning, and Y5 a digital-skills proxy) and two contextual variables (Z1 unemployment and Z2 citizenship) at NUTS-I and country levels. The robust BoD model benchmarks regions against a best-practice frontier, while the robust conditional BoD reweights comparisons using contextual similarity (kernel-based sampling) to produce more equitable peer sets and realistic targets. Results show substantial differences between robust and conditional scores (e.g., conditional scores generally higher), with only 8 super-performers in the robust regional analysis and 35 conditional peers identified. Limitations include reliance on cross-sectional 2019 data, incomplete indicator coverage at granular level (excluding a PISA-supported basic-skills indicator), and the absence of explicit missing-data handling details beyond a complete-data requirement. data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse for ML-related fields because the article is a methodological benchmarking study using Data Envelopment Analysis/Benefit-of-the-Doubt composite indicators rather than an empirical predictive ML model. It does not train or evaluate supervised ML algorithms, and it does not use ILSA PV-based achievement outcomes; therefore, PV handling, missing-data handling specifics, and ML technique lists are not applicable in the schema sense. The study’s core outputs are composite efficiency/benchmark scores and peer intensities derived from optimization under robust and robust-conditional formulations.
